title: Food when the power goes out
summary: Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. A fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours; a full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24. Eat the most perishable food first, move fridge food into a cooler with ice after 4 hours, and never put food outside to keep it cold, even in winter. Check food in Is it still good? before you eat or refreeze it.
doFirst: Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. With the doors shut, a fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours and a half-full freezer about 24 hours (CDC, FoodSafety.gov, USDA).
Eat the most perishable food first: leftovers, meat, poultry, and foods with milk, cream, sour cream or soft cheese (New York State Department of Health).
Power out for 4 hours and you have a cooler and ice? Put the fridge’s perishable food in the cooler, with ice or frozen gel packs, to keep it at 40°F (4°C) or below (CDC).
Don’t put food outside to keep it cold, even in winter (New York State Department of Health). Make ice outside instead (USDA).
Before you eat, cook or refreeze anything, check it in Is it still good? Never taste food to find out if it is safe (CDC).

blocks.p: Times for a power outage, from CDC, FoodSafety.gov and USDA. New York State Department of Health gives the same: a fully filled freezer stays at freezing for about two days, a half-full one stays cold for about one day.

blocks.cap: Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. With the doors shut, a fridge keeps food cold for about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours and a half-full freezer about 24 hours (CDC, FoodSafety.gov, USDA). Before you eat, cook or refreeze anything, check it in Is it still good?

list: Open the doors only as much as you must to check the temperature quickly and get your food (New York State Department of Health).

In the freezer, group items together so they form an “igloo” and protect each other (New York State Department of Health). When the freezer is not full, keep items close together: it helps the food stay cold longer (USDA).
Keep meat together on one side of the freezer or on a tray, so that if it begins to thaw its juices don’t get on other food (New York State Department of Health).
Food with a lot of water in it, such as meat or fruit, stays frozen longer than food with little water, such as bread (New York State Department of Health).
Put ice or frozen water containers in the fridge or freezer to keep the food cold (New York State Department of Health).
If you think the power will be out for a long time, get block ice for the fridge or freezer (CDC, New York State Department of Health).

If the power has been out for 4 hours and you have a cooler and ice, put the fridge’s perishable food in the cooler. Add ice or a cold source like frozen gel packs to keep it at 40°F (4°C) or below (CDC).
In freezing weather, make ice: fill buckets, empty milk cartons or cans with water and leave them outside to freeze. Then put the ice in your fridge, freezer or coolers (USDA).

blocks.warn: Don’t put your food outside to keep it cold, even in the winter (New York State Department of Health).

list: Weather cold enough for fridge food is too warm for frozen food (New York State Department of Health).
Even when it is very cold outside, the sun can warm food enough for germs to grow, and frozen food can thaw in the sun (New York State Department of Health, USDA).
The temperature outside can change hour by hour; it will not protect fridge or freezer food (USDA).
Animals can get into food and contaminate it (New York State Department of Health). Never eat food that has come in contact with an animal (USDA).
Keep an appliance thermometer in the fridge and in the freezer (CDC, New York State Department of Health).
The fridge should be at 40°F (4°C) or below, and the freezer at 0°F (-18°C) or below (CDC).
Not sure a particular food is cold enough? Take its temperature with a food thermometer (USDA).

sections.h: After 4 hours, or when the power comes back

blocks.p: What to keep, what to refreeze and what to throw out, food by food, is in Is it still good? Check each food separately (FoodSafety.gov). When in doubt, throw it out (CDC).

sections.h: A generator for the fridge or freezer

blocks.p: A generator can keep a fridge or freezer running. Read Generators before you use one. Its first rule: “Run it only outside, more than 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointing away from the house (CDC, CPSC).”

list: Keep appliance thermometers in the fridge and freezer (CDC).
Freeze containers of water and gel packs to help keep food at 40°F (4°C) or below (CDC).
Have a cooler and frozen gel packs ready in case you have to take food out of the fridge to keep it cold (CDC).
Keep food on hand that needs no refrigeration and can be eaten cold or heated on an outdoor grill (USDA). Keep a hand-held can opener (USDA).
